        REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO CONSOLIDATE CASES AND APPOINT INTERIM LEAD COUNSEL
                                       Case No. 4:25-CV-2095
  1                                           I.         INTRODUCTION

 2          As noted in Plaintiffs’ opening motion, appointing both Tycko & Zavareei LLP and Sauder

 3 Schelkopf LLC as Interim Co-Lead Counsel serves the best interests of the proposed class. This co-lead

 4 structure is well-supported by precedent and ensures the case is staffed with experienced firms that can

 5 efficiently share resources, divide labor, and mitigate litigation risk—particularly in a complex, high-

 6 stakes testing software failure case impacting potentially thousands of class members.

 7                                                II.    ARGUMENT

 8 A.       Co-Leadership Structure Is Appropriate and Well-Supported by Precedent

 9          Defendant’s assertion that co-leadership inherently leads to inefficiency overlooks the practical

10 benefits of collaboration between firms with demonstrated success in nationwide class actions. In a case

11 involving strikingly similar facts, the court appointed five firms to serve as class counsel. West v.

12 ExamSoft Worldwide Inc., No. 1:14-cv-22950, Dkt. 37 (S.D. Fla. May 12, 2015) (Ungaro, J.) (certifying

13 nationwide settlement class in a consumer software malfunction case arising from ExamSoft’s failure

14 during the July 2014 bar exam, preliminarily approving settlement, and appointing five firms as class

15 counsel).

16          This Court and Courts in this District1 and across the country have routinely approved the

17 appointment of multiple firms as co-lead counsel where doing so promotes effective case management

18 and ensures adequate representation. See, e.g., Aberin, et al., v. Am. Honda Motor Co. Inc., No. 16-cv-

19 04384, 2017 WL 3641793 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 24, 2017) (Tigar, J.) (appointing two firms as interim class

20 counsel); Tabak v. Apple Inc., No. 4:19-cv-02455, Dkt. 176 at 1 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 21, 2023) (Tigar, J.)

21
     1
22     See In re Uber Techs., Passenger Sexual Assault Litig., MDL No. 3084, Dkt. 152 (N.D. Cal. Dec.
     6,2023) (Breyer, J.) (appointing multiple firms as co-lead counsel and establishing a Plaintiffs' Steering
23   Committee to manage nationwide class litigation). Frasco v. Flo Health Inc., No. 3:21-cv-00757-JD,
     Dkt. 80 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 12, 2021) (Donato, J.) (appointing two firms as co-lead counsel in a data privacy
24   class action regarding unauthorized data sharing with third parties). In re Anthem, Inc. Data Breach
25   Litig., No. 15-MD-02617-LHK, Dkt. 284 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 11, 2015) (Koh, J.) (appointing several firms
     to lead roles in data breach MDL). In re Facebook, Inc. Consumer Privacy User Profile Litig., 3:18-md-
26   02843, Dkt. 102(N.D. Cal. Jul. 27, 2018) (Chhabria, J.) (appointing two firms as co-lead counsel in
     privacy litigation).
27

28
         REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO CONSOLIDATE CASES AND APPOINT INTERIM LEAD COUNSEL
                                        Case No. 4:25-CV-2095
  1 (appointing two firms, including Tycko & Zavareei, LLP, as class counsel). In re Wells Fargo & Co.

 2 S’holder Derivative Litig., No. 3:16-cv-05541, Dkt. 312 at 2-3 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 7, 2020) (Tigar, J.)

 3 (appointing multiple law firms to lead role in shareholder derivative case resulting in historic $240

 4 million settlement); In re Plantronics, Inc. Sec. Litig., No. 4:19-cv-07481-JST, Dkt. 62 at 3 (N.D. Cal.

 5 2020) (Tigar, J.) (appointing two firms as co-leads in securities fraud action).

 6 B.       The Proposed Structure Will Promote Efficiency and Adequate Representation

 7          The structure Plaintiffs propose is neither unusual nor excessive. Rather, it reflects the realities

 8 of modern complex litigation, where the volume of discovery, the number of class members, and the

 9 technical nature of the issues benefit from multiple firms with complementary experience and capacity.

10 This case involves issues requiring substantial technical expertise and the resources of more than one

11 firm. Appointing two firms to lead this matter ensures appropriate staffing levels without unnecessary

12 duplication and provides built-in checks to avoid overstaffing or inefficiencies. Defendant has not

13 offered any factual or legal support for its contention that appointing two firms will lead to bloat, as

14 there is none.

15          Moreover, the proposed co-lead counsel have already demonstrated a strong collaborative

16 working relationship. As reflected in the record, they have jointly investigated the claims, coordinated

17 communications with related plaintiffs, and taken the lead in moving this litigation forward. This

18 cooperation will continue under the co-lead structure and will only enhance the quality and efficiency

19 of representation. Significantly, the Proposed Interim Co-Lead Counsel have worked cooperatively in

20 the past. See, e.g., Gorzo, et al. v. Rodan & Fields, LLC, No. CJC-18-004981 (Cal. Superior Court, San.

21 Francisco County) (approving $38 million settlement where Sauder Schelkopf LLC and Tycko &

22 Zavareei LLP served as class counsel).

23 C.       Paragraph 4 of the Proposed Order Should Not Be Stricken

24          Defendant also requests the Court strike Paragraph 4 of Plaintiffs’ Proposed Order, which states:

25 “Additional related cases filed, transferred, or removed to this District will be consolidated with this

26 action.” ECF No. 16-3, at ¶ 4. Defendant admits that “consolidation likely will be appropriate for a

27 related case filed in, transferred to, or removed to this District,” but argues that “a preemptive, blanket
                                                         2
28
       REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO CONSOLIDATE CASES AND APPOINT INTERIM LEAD COUNSEL
                                              Case No. 4:25-CV-2095
  1 order is not necessary.” ECF No. 31, at 2. Striking Paragraph 4, however, would undermine the central

 2 purpose of the leadership order, which is to provide clarity on who can prosecute the litigation and

 3 negotiate on behalf of the proposed class. If there were no obligation to consolidate related cases, other

 4 counsel would be permitted to engage in the duties and responsibilities in Paragraph 7, thus

 5 circumventing the leadership order and impeding the undersigned counsel’s authority. Plaintiffs

 6 respectfully request that the Court reject Defendant’s request to strike Paragraph 4.

 7                                            III.   CONCLUSION

 8          Defendant does not oppose consolidation and does not oppose appointment of interim lead

 9 counsel. As its challenge to appointing two well-qualified firms is unsupported and wrong, Plaintiffs

10 request that the Court grant Plaintiffs’ Motion and enter Plaintiffs’ proposed order.

           PROCTORU, INC.’S MEMORANDUM IN PARTIAL OPPOSITION TO PLAINTIFFS’ MOTION TO
                      CONSOLIDATE CASES AND APPOINT INTERIM LEAD COUNSEL
                                                   1
       Case 4:25-cv-02095-JST           Document 31         Filed 04/24/25      Page 2 of 5



 1                                            INTRODUCTION

 2           Plaintiffs’ Motion includes two requests for relief. First, Plaintiffs ask this Court to

 3   consolidate this Perjanik action and Trisha A.M. v. ProctorU, Inc. d/b/a Meazure Learning, No.

 4   25-cv-02197-JST (N.D. Cal.), which is a related action that is also pending before this Court, for

 5   pretrial proceedings. Meazure Learning does not oppose Plaintiffs’ request for consolidation.

 6           Second, Plaintiffs request that the Court appoint attorneys from two law firms—Tycko &

 7   Zavareei LLP and Sauder Schelkopf LLC—as “Interim Co-Lead Counsel.” Meazure Learning

 8   does not oppose the appointment of interim lead counsel, and Meazure Learning would not object

 9   to either law firm serving in that role. Plaintiffs, however, have made no showing that the

10   appointment of two law firms as interim co-lead counsel is necessary or would be efficient.

11   Accordingly, Meazure Learning opposes Plaintiffs’ request to have both firms appointed as interim

12   co-lead counsel.

13           Finally, in their Proposed Order (ECF 16-3), Plaintiffs propose that the Court order that

14   “[a]dditional related cases filed, transferred, or removed to this District will be consolidated with

15   this action.” (ECF 16-3, Proposed Order ¶ 4, p. 1.) Although Meazure Learning anticipates that

16   consolidation likely will be appropriate for a related case filed in, transferred to, or removed to this

17   District, a preemptive, blanket order is not necessary. Paragraph 4 of Plaintiffs’ Proposed Order

18   should be struck.

19                                               ARGUMENT

20   I.      Consolidation of the Perjanik Action and the Trisha A.M. Action

21           Meazure Learning does not oppose Plaintiffs’ request to consolidate this Perjanik action

22   and the Trisha A.M. action for pretrial proceedings.

23   II.     Appointment of Interim Co-Lead Counsel

24           Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(g)(3), a “court may designate interim counsel to

25   act on behalf of a putative class before determining whether to certify the action as a class action.”

26   Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(g)(3). “Although Rule 23(g)(3) does not provide a standard for appointment of

27   interim counsel, courts in this district typically consider the factors set forth in 23(g)(1).” In re

28   Meta Pixel Healthcare Litig., No. 22-cv-03580-WHO, 2022 WL 18399978, at *2 (N.D. Cal.

           PROCTORU, INC.’S MEMORANDUM IN PARTIAL OPPOSITION TO PLAINTIFFS’ MOTION TO
                      CONSOLIDATE CASES AND APPOINT INTERIM LEAD COUNSEL
                                                       2
          Case 4:25-cv-02095-JST        Document 31         Filed 04/24/25      Page 3 of 5



 1   Dec. 21, 2022); Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(g)(1)(A) (“In appointing class counsel, the court . . . must

 2   consider: (i) the work counsel has done in identifying or investigating potential claims in the action;

 3   (ii) counsel’s experience in handling class actions, other complex litigation, and the types of claims

 4   asserted in the action; (iii) counsel’s knowledge of the applicable law; and (iv) the resources that

 5   counsel will commit to representing the class.”).

 6            The advisory committee’s notes to Rule 23 state that a “the court should be alert to the need

 7   for adequate staffing of the case, but also to the risk of overstaffing or an ungainly counsel

 8   structure.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 23 advisory committee’s notes to 2003 amendment. 1

 9            “[A] single firm will usually provide more effective and efficient representation than a

10   group of two or more firms.” In re Cathode Ray Tubes (CRT) Antitrust Litig., No. 07-cv-5944,

11   2008 WL 2024957, at *1 (N.D. Cal. May 9, 2008); see also Nicolow v. Hewlett Packard Co., No.

12   12-cv-5980, 2013 WL 792642, at *9 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 4, 2013) (“This Court agrees with other district

13   courts that have acknowledged the tendency of shared leadership structures to complicate, muddle,

14   and otherwise bloat litigation.”). As the court explained in In re Cathode Ray Tubes, “[a] single

15   firm is already organized with internal levels of communication and management structure” but

16   “[a] group of firms, on the other hand, must create these structures.” 2008 WL 2024957, at *1.

17   “This will tend to increase the risk that items may fall through the cracks.” Id. Similarly, in In re

18   Allergan PLC Securities Litigation, the court noted that “the involvement of multiple firms tends

19   to inflate legal fees to the detriment of the other class members.” No. 18-cv-12089, 2020 WL

20   5796763, at *6 (S.D.N.Y. Sept. 29, 2020).

21

22

23
     1
       See also Manual for Complex Litigation § 10.224, pp. 27–28 (4th ed. 2004, 3d printing 2020)
24   (“Deferring to proposals by counsel without independent examination, even those that seem to have
     the concurrence of a majority of those affected, invites problems down the road if designated
25   counsel turn out to be unwilling or unable to discharge their responsibilities satisfactorily or if they
26   incur excessive costs . . . The court should inquire as to normal or anticipated billing rates, define
     record-keeping requirements, and establish guidelines, methods, or limitations to govern the award
27   of fees. While it may be appropriate and possibly even beneficial for several firms to divide work
     among themselves, such an arrangement should be necessary, not simply the result of a bargain
28   among the attorneys.”).

           PROCTORU, INC.’S MEMORANDUM IN PARTIAL OPPOSITION TO PLAINTIFFS’ MOTION TO
                      CONSOLIDATE CASES AND APPOINT INTERIM LEAD COUNSEL
                                                       3
       Case 4:25-cv-02095-JST          Document 31         Filed 04/24/25     Page 4 of 5



 1          “Where there is no demonstrable need for more than one class counsel, courts reject such

 2   applications.” Fan v. PHL Variable Life Ins. Co., No. 18-cv-1288, 2019 WL 10948633, at *3

 3   (S.D.N.Y. May 29, 2019).

 4          Here, Plaintiffs state that the two proposed law firms “have worked cooperatively to

 5   determine the best and most efficient course of action with regard to consolidating these actions

 6   and moving the case forward expeditiously.” (ECF 16, Mot. 6.) Plaintiffs, however, do not identify

 7   any reason why it is necessary or appropriate for two law firms to be appointed as interim co-lead

 8   counsel. If two law firms were to serve as interim co-lead counsel, there would be a risk of

 9   “overstaffing,” Fed. R. Civ. P. 23 advisory committee’s notes to 2003 amendment, and “inflate[d]

10   legal fees,” In re Allergan PLC, 2020 WL 5796763, at *6. Meazure Learning opposes the

11   appointment of two law firms as interim co-lead counsel but would not object to the appointment

12   of either law firm to serve as interim lead counsel in the consolidated case.

13                                            CONCLUSION

14          In sum: (1) Meazure Learning does not oppose the consolidation of this Perjanik action

15   and the Trisha A.M. action for pretrial proceedings; (2) Meazure Learning does oppose the

16   appointment of two firms to serve as interim co-lead counsel, but Meazure Learning would not

17   object to either firm—Tycko & Zavareei LLP and Sauder Schelkopf LLC—serving as interim lead

18   counsel in the consolidated action; and (3) Paragraph 4 of Plaintiffs’ Proposed Order (ECF 16-3),

19   which concerns prospective consolidation of actions filed in, removed to, or transferred to this

20   District, should be struck.
